guidelines.summary: Know and document every implementation-defined behaviour the program relies on.
All source files must build without compilation errors.
Code should be traceable to documented requirements.
Keep the risk of run-time failures as low as possible.
Document any use of assembly language.
Keep assembly language isolated and wrapped (e.g. in functions or macros).
Do not leave blocks of code disabled by turning them into comments.
Identifiers visible at the same time should not look alike.
Prefer typedefs that state size and signedness over the plain numeric types.
Check the error information a function returns.
Hide the layout of structures that a translation unit never needs to look inside.
Prefer functions to function-like macros where either would do.
Guard header files against multiple inclusion.
Check arguments before passing them to library functions.
Avoid dynamic memory allocation.
Call functions that operate on a resource in the correct order.
Validate data that comes from outside the program.
Handle floating-point infinities and NaNs explicitly.
Prevent data races on objects shared between threads.
Prevent deadlocks between threads.
Do not create threads dynamically.
Stay within the C language: no syntax or constraint errors and no translation limits exceeded.
Avoid compiler-specific language extensions.
Do not rely on undefined or critical unspecified behaviour.
Avoid the newer language features the guidelines flag as emergent.
Avoid language features marked obsolescent in the C standard.
No code that can never be reached.
No operations whose removal would not change program behaviour (dead code).
No type declarations that are never used.
No tag declarations that are never used.
No macro definitions that are never used.
No labels that are never used.
No function parameters that are never used.
No object definitions that are never used.
Do not nest comment openers inside a comment.
Do not continue a // comment onto the next line with a backslash.
End octal and hexadecimal escape sequences unambiguously.
Do not use trigraphs.
Identifiers with external linkage must be distinguishable.
Identifiers in the same scope and name space must be distinguishable.
Do not hide an outer-scope identifier with an inner declaration.
Macro names must be distinguishable from each other.
Do not reuse a macro name as another identifier.
Each typedef name is used for one type only.
Each tag name is used for one type only.
Names of objects and functions with external linkage are not reused.
Names of objects and functions with internal linkage should not be reused.
Declare bit-fields only with suitable types.
A one-bit named bit-field must be unsigned.
Do not put bit-fields in unions.
Do not write octal integer constants.
Mark integer constants that have an unsigned type with a U suffix.
Use an upper-case L, never a lower-case l, in literal suffixes.
Only assign string literals to pointers to const char.
Give integer-constant macros an argument of the right form.
Do not use the minimum-width constant macros for the small integer types.
Always state types explicitly (no implicit int).
Declare functions with full prototypes that name their parameters.
All declarations of an object or function use the same names and qualifiers.
Make a compatible declaration visible before defining an externally linked object or function.
Declare an external object or function once, in one file.
An externally linked identifier has exactly one definition.
Do not give external linkage to something used in only one translation unit.
Use static on every declaration of an internally linked object or function.
Define an object at block scope if only one function uses it.
Declare inline functions static.
Give externally linked arrays an explicit size.
Implicitly valued enumeration constants must not duplicate another value in the list.
Point to const-qualified types whenever the pointee is not modified.
Do not use the restrict qualifier.
Every declaration of an explicitly aligned object specifies the same alignment.
Do not specify an alignment of zero.
Use at most one explicit alignment specifier per declaration.
Do not read an automatic object before it has been given a value.
Brace the initializer of an aggregate or union.
Do not initialise only part of an array.
Do not initialise the same element twice.
Size arrays explicitly when designated initializers are used.
Do not mix chained designators with undesignated initializers.
Initialise atomic objects properly before they are accessed.
Operands must have an essential type that suits the operator.
Use character-typed operands in additions and subtractions only in sensible ways.
Do not assign a value to a narrower essential type or a different essential type category.
Operands of an arithmetic operator that balances types should share an essential type category.
Avoid casts to an inappropriate essential type.
Do not assign a composite expression to a wider essential type.
Do not widen the other operand of an operator whose operand is a composite expression.
Do not cast a composite expression to a wider type or a different category.
No conversions between function pointers and any other type.
No conversions between pointers to incomplete types and any other type.
No casts between pointers to different object types.
Avoid conversions between pointers and integers.
Avoid converting void pointers into object pointers.
No casts between void pointers and arithmetic types.
No casts between object pointers and non-integer arithmetic types.
Do not cast away const, volatile or _Atomic qualification.
Write null pointer constants only as NULL.
Do not apply _Atomic to void.
Make operator precedence explicit with parentheses.
Keep shift amounts within the width of the left operand's essential type.
Avoid the comma operator.
Avoid unsigned wrap-around when evaluating constant expressions.
Do not apply sizeof to a parameter declared as an array.
Do not access members of atomic structures or unions directly.
Initializer lists must not have persistent side effects.
An expression's value and side effects must not depend on evaluation order.
Keep ++ and -- out of expressions that have other side effects.
Do not use the result of an assignment as a value.
The right operand of && or || must not have persistent side effects.
The operand of sizeof must not have side effects.
Loop counters must not be floating-point.
Write for loops in a well-formed shape.
Controlling expressions must not be invariant.
if and loop conditions must be essentially Boolean.
Avoid goto.
goto may only jump forward within the same function.
goto may only jump to a label in the same or an enclosing block.
Leave a loop through at most one break or goto.
Prefer a single exit point at the end of a function.
Loop and selection bodies must be compound statements (braced).
End every if ... else if chain with a final else.
Write switch statements in a well-formed shape.
Place switch labels only directly in the switch body.
End every switch clause with an unconditional break.
Give every switch a default label.
Put the default label first or last.
A switch needs at least two clauses.
Do not switch on an essentially Boolean expression.
Do not use the <stdarg.h> facilities.
No direct or indirect recursion.
Never call a function that has not been declared.
Every exit path of a non-void function returns a value.
Pass array arguments with enough elements for the parameter.
Do not put static inside the brackets of an array parameter.
Use the value returned by a non-void function.
Do not modify function parameters.
A _Noreturn function must not return.
A _Noreturn function must have a void return type.
Declare functions that never return as _Noreturn.
Use a function name only to call it or with &.
Do not qualify function types.
Pointer arithmetic must stay within the same array.
Subtract pointers only when they point into the same array.
Compare pointers relationally only within the same object.
Avoid +, -, += and -= on pointers.
Use at most two levels of pointer indirection in declarations.
Do not let the address of an automatic or thread-local object outlive it.
Do not declare flexible array members.
Do not use variable-length arrays.
Do not convert an array with temporary lifetime into a pointer.
Do not use pointers to variably-modified array types.
Do not copy or assign an object onto storage that overlaps it.
Avoid unions.
Put #include directives before any code.
Keep quote, backslash and comment characters out of header file names.
#include must be followed by <file> or "file".
Do not define macros named like keywords.
Avoid #undef.
Do not put directive-like tokens inside macro arguments.
Parenthesise macro parameters when they are expanded in expressions.
#if and #elif conditions must evaluate to 0 or 1.
Define identifiers before using them in #if or #elif.
Avoid the # and ## preprocessor operators.
Do not follow a stringised parameter directly with ##.
A parameter used with # or ## must not also be macro-expanded elsewhere in the body.
Lines starting with # must be valid preprocessing directives.
Keep #else, #elif and #endif in the same file as their #if.
Do not #define or #undef reserved identifiers or macros.
Do not declare reserved identifiers or macro names.
Do not use the <stdlib.h> allocation and deallocation functions.
Do not use <setjmp.h>.
Do not use <signal.h>.
Do not use the standard library input/output functions.
Do not use the ato* string conversion functions.
Do not use the <stdlib.h> program termination functions.
Do not use bsearch or qsort.
Do not use the standard time and date functions.
Do not use <tgmath.h>.
Avoid the floating-point exception features of <fenv.h>.
Pass <ctype.h> functions only unsigned char values or EOF.
Do not compare null-terminated strings with memcmp.
memcpy, memmove and memcmp take pointers to compatible types.
Use memcmp only on suitable types (pointer, integer, Boolean, enum).
<string.h> functions must not read or write out of bounds.
size_t arguments to <string.h> functions must be in range.
Treat pointers from localeconv, getenv, setlocale and strerror as pointers to const.
Do not use a pointer from asctime, getenv and similar after calling the same function again.
Do not call system.
Type-generic math macros need operands of a suitable essential type.
Operands of multi-argument type-generic math macros share one standard type.
Do not use rand or srand.
Use only sequentially consistent memory ordering.
Call mtx_timedlock only on mutexes that support timeouts.
Release every resource that was acquired dynamically.
Free only memory obtained from the standard allocation functions.
Do not open one file for reading and writing on separate streams at the same time.
Do not write to a read-only stream.
Do not dereference a FILE pointer.
Do not use a FILE pointer after its stream has been closed.
Compare EOF only with the unmodified result of a function that can return it.
Set errno to zero before calling a function that sets it.
Test errno after calling a function that sets it.
Test errno only right after a function that sets it.
Join or detach a thread at most once.
Access thread, synchronisation and TSS objects only through their library functions.
Give thread, synchronisation and TSS objects a suitable storage duration.
Initialise synchronisation objects before use.
Destroy synchronisation and TSS objects only after every thread using them has finished.
A thread unlocks every mutex it locks.
Only unlock, or wait on, a mutex that the calling thread holds.
Do not lock a non-recursive mutex twice.
Use a condition variable with one mutex only.
Create thread-specific storage before accessing it.
Use generic selections only inside macro expansions.
A generic selection written outside a macro must have no side effects in its controlling expression.
A generic selection should list at least one non-default association.
Associations in a generic selection must use suitable types.
Generic selections should not rely on implicit pointer conversions.
The controlling expression's essential type must match its standard type.
A macro containing a generic selection evaluates its argument once.
Put the default association first or last.
No statements that can never be reached.
Controlling expressions should not be invariant.
Avoid writing values to local objects that are never read afterwards.
Use the value a function returns.
Locally visible variables should be used.
Named function parameters must be used.
Locally visible types should be used.
Locally visible functions should be used.
Use floating-point arithmetic with care.
Respect the preconditions of the functions you call.
Conform to ISO C++17.
Avoid deprecated language features.
Do not rely on undefined or critical unspecified behaviour.
Sequence accesses to the same memory location correctly.
Avoid character sequences that look like trigraphs.
Do not nest /* inside a C-style comment.
Do not leave code disabled by commenting it out.
Do not continue a // comment with a backslash.
Do not write octal integer constants.
Suffix unsigned integer literals with U.
Use an upper-case L, never a lower-case l, to start a literal suffix.
Do not violate the one-definition rule.
Do not hide an outer-scope variable with an inner declaration.
Do not access an object outside its lifetime.
Do not return a pointer or reference to a local automatic object.
Use nullptr as the only null pointer constant.
Do not use C-style or functional-notation casts.
Pointer arithmetic must not create an invalid pointer.
Subtract pointers only within the same array.
Compare pointers relationally only within the same array.
Do not copy an object onto storage that overlaps it.
Loop and selection bodies must be compound statements (braced).
Avoid goto.
A non-void function returns a value on every path.
Const-qualify the pointee of pointer and reference parameters where possible.
Avoid declaring C-style arrays.
Do not read an object before it has been set.
Use virtual, override and final consistently on member functions.
Do not use an object's dynamic type while it is being constructed or destroyed.
Make single-argument constructors and conversion operators explicit.
Initialise all non-static data members before the object can be used.
User-written copy and move assignment operators must cope with self-assignment.
Do not put directive-like tokens inside macro arguments.
Avoid dynamic memory.
Manage dynamic memory automatically (RAII), not by hand.
Do not use <cstdarg>.
Do not use <csetjmp>.
Do not use the facilities of <csignal>.
Do not use an object that may have been moved from.
Use the result of std::remove, std::remove_if, std::unique and empty().
Do not use the C library input/output functions.
Do not assign values to non-volatile variables that are never read afterwards.
No code that can never be reached.
Use the value a non-void function returns.
No paths that can never be taken.
No variables that are never used.
No dead code.
Every defined function should be called.
Do not copy an object onto storage that overlaps it.
Do not hide an identifier from an outer scope.
Do not violate the one-definition rule.
Declare identifiers in the smallest block scope possible.
Use the fixed-width integer typedefs instead of the basic numeric types.
Use only nullptr as the null pointer constant.
Conditions of if and loop statements must have type bool.
Pointer arithmetic must stay within the same array.
Subtract pointers only within the same array.
Compare pointers relationally only within the same array.
Avoid unexplained literal values; use named constants.
Do not use C-style casts.
Do not access arrays or containers out of bounds.
Do not dereference null pointers.
The divisor must not be zero.
Keep shift amounts within the width of the left operand.
Do not use the comma operator.
switch, while, do and for bodies must be compound statements (braced).
if and else bodies must be compound statements (braced).
End every switch with a default clause.
Do not use goto.
Do not use typedef; prefer using aliases.
Do not return a reference or pointer to a parameter passed by reference to const.
Do not define variadic functions with an ellipsis.
A non-void function returns a value on every path.
Initialise all memory before reading it.
Do not use unions.
Declare a virtual function with exactly one of virtual, override or final.
Constructors must initialise all base classes and non-static data members.
Do not use an object's dynamic type in its constructor or destructor.
Make constructors callable with one fundamental-type argument explicit.
Do not read an object after it has been moved from.
Do not leak resources when an exception is thrown.
A noexcept function must not throw.
Do not put directive-like tokens inside macro arguments.
Do not use abort, exit, getenv or system from <cstdlib>.
Do not use the <ctime> time functions.
Do not use the unbounded <cstring> functions.
Do not use C-style arrays.
Do not use malloc, calloc, realloc or free.
Do not call non-placement new or delete expressions directly.
Match each form of new with the corresponding form of delete.
Do not use errno.
Do not let more than one smart pointer own the same raw pointer.
Do not use iterators, pointers or references a container has invalidated.
Do not use the <cstdio> stream functions.
